Business.title: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions unanswered
Business.text:
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

Business.title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
Business.text:
Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.

Here's what you need to know about the payment.

For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.

A typical yearly energy bill is forecast to jump by £276 in January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.

And some more recent forecasts suggest a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January.

Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.

Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.

As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in, external. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.

If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.

The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.

He urged the devolved governments to follow suit to "give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter".

The Welsh government has said that it will also make a £100 cost-of-living payment to all households in council tax bands A to D.

The Scottish government said it would "seek to replicate" the £100 energy payment.

Meanwhile, the Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.

If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.

Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.

However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.

Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way of giving them the payments.

This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.

The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.

The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

Business.title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
Business.text:
Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.

John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.

The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.

But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.

Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.

It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.

The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.

They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.

By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.

The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.

However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax.

The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary, external.

National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.

Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.

Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.

However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.

How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.

There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.

Business.title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
Business.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.

The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.

Anthropic also detailed some of the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.

Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.

Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.

Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.

But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.

Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.

Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.

The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.

Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.

"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.

Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.

At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.

Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.

Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.

The leasing of data centres alone is set to cost the company $321.4bn through agreements struck so far this year.

Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.

Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.

Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.

A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10m in the past year.

An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".

The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.

Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.

Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".

The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.

For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.

"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.

That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission."

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice, and making more efficient power grids and batteries.

Anthropic said AI could one day provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.

"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

Business.title: Data centre backlash grows ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
Business.text:
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

Business.title: Fed Holds Rates Steady Despite ‘Elevated’ Inflation
Business.text:
In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Warsh said the Fed would meet eight times next year as usual. But only seven of those meetings will include a vote on interest rates. The eighth “will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy,” he said.

In 2028, the Fed expects to hold just six rate-setting meetings, with two meetings dedicated to discussions of longer-run strategy, Mr. Warsh said.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said, “but it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”

Some economists have criticized the idea of holding fewer meetings, arguing it could make it harder for the Fed to respond quickly to changes in inflation and the labor market. The move also fits a pattern during the early months of Mr. Warsh’s chairmanship toward providing less information to investors and the public, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater openness.

Other economists, however, have defended the idea. They argue that providing more time between meetings will make it easier for policymakers to identify meaningful shifts in economic conditions. And they note that the Fed can hold emergency meetings if necessary, as it has done numerous times in the past.

Sports.title: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
Sports.text:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who landed in Miami after losing the presidential election on Sunday, has said it was never his intention to "leave my homeland".

"I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil," he said in his first statement since his departure.

The US provided visas to him and his family after Brazil cancelled his passports as part of a criminal investigation. Bolsonaro denies any wrongdoing. On Wednesday, US President Donald Trump told reporters: "We gave him a pass to come into the country".

Newly re-elected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised Bolsonaro's secretive exit from the country, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

In a statement, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country".

"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said. "I departed from a regime of exception so that I could become the leader my people deserve."

He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.

In the lengthy letter, he also repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.

On Wednesday, Trump declined to discuss the allegations made in Bolsonaro's letter.

"I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," Trump said. He went on to add that he thought Bolsonaro "and his family were treated very unfairly".

After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.

The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, who was appointed by Bolsonaro's father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.

For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low-profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday, in addition to a criminal investigation that led to orders that his passports be turned into authorities.

But when he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline on Tuesday, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.

Speculation quickly grew that he'd left the country and Bolsonaro's lawyers said they had no idea where he was.

Sports.title: Estevao: Why is the Brazilian becoming Chelsea's forgotten man?
Sports.text:
The last time Chelsea beat Liverpool, Estevao was the talk of the Premier League.

The Brazilian was still in his first couple of months at Stamford Bridge when his name hit the headlines after he scored the winner against the Premier League champions with practically the final kick of the match last October.

Fast forward 12 months, and Estevao is beginning to attract attention for all the wrong reasons as he struggles to force his way into Xabi Alonso's side.

The 19-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Palmeiras last summer, was conspicuous by his absence on Wednesday night as Chelsea were knocked out of the Carabao Cup following a penalty shootout loss to Liverpool at Anfield.

The Blues had taken the lead in the first half through Morgan Rogers, but they failed to kick on after Cody Gakpo quickly restored parity for the hosts.

Most concerning for Estevao, though, was that as both teams pushed for a winner in the second half, Alonso never appeared to consider the forward.

The clearest indication of just how low Estevao sits in Alonso's pecking order came midway through the second half, when Alonso made a triple substitution in an attempt to turn the game in his side's favour.

One of the three changes was Emanuel Emegha, who had yet to feature for the Blues since his summer move from Strasbourg.

Just moments after that triple change, which brought Chelsea's total number of substitutions to five, Estevao could be seen ending his warm-up and retreating to the bench.

It was another night of no action for the Brazilian.

Sadly for Estevao, Wednesday night's situation at Anfield was nothing new for him.

The Brazilian has failed to make the starting XI in any of the eight Premier League matches since Alonso took charge of the Blues in the summer.

His total minutes for the campaign so far stand at an underwhelming 172, with 125 of those coming in the victories over Luton Town and Leeds United in the earlier rounds of the EFL Cup.

Yet even in the thrilling 6-3 win against Daniel Farke's side, which remains one of only two games he has started this campaign, he was withdrawn at half-time with Chelsea trailing 1-0.

After the fourth-round defeat by Liverpool, Alonso defended his decision not to play Estevao, hinting that the forward is still coming to grips with the physical demands of English football.

"We started with Pedro [Neto], Morgan [Rogers] and Danny Welbeck, and the game had very intense moments," said Alonso.

"We knew it was going to be physical, and Malo [Gusto] had cramps, so we were a bit forced with substitutions. The season is going to be very long, and there will be moments for everyone."

When asked directly about the Brazilian, Alonso added: "He could be happier. He wants to play. I'm sure Estevao will have his moment, it is my responsibility.

"We know the game in England is really intense, and you need to be up for it. Estevao is in his second season. The season is going to be long."

One of the main reasons behind Estevao's exile has been the form of Pedro Neto.

It was only a couple of months ago that Portugal international Neto looked destined to leave Chelsea, only two years after joining from Wolverhampton Wanderers.

The 26-year-old was linked with a move to Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, but he ultimately remained at Stamford Bridge.

That decision appears to have been influenced by Alonso, who has underlined his faith in Neto by handing him seven starts in eight Premier League matches this season.

His success out on the right - which also happens to be Estevao's favoured position - has meant opportunities have been few and far between for the Brazilian.

He has primarily been deployed as a right-sided wing-back in Alonso's 3-4-2-1 system, with his Premier League experience and greater defensive solidity compared to Estevao seemingly winning over the Spaniard.

After an impressive start to the campaign, in which he has scored four goals in 11 matches, Neto was rewarded with a new six-year deal at Stamford Bridge.

"He's a player who is a little bit of a victim of the system," former Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff told Sky Sports.

"Alonso tends to play Neto in that hybrid wing-back role, expecting him to get high up the pitch as well. Maybe he doesn't feel that suits Estevao, and I don't feel it does either."

One area that has not been a problem for the Blues this season is attack, with the forward positions firmly in the hands of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Rogers, who has made a spectacular start to life at Stamford Bridge following his £117m move from Aston Villa.

Against Liverpool, though, Estevao couldn't even get a look-in despite Chelsea being without the suspended Palmer and the injured Joao Pedro.

"How Estevao has not got on the pitch tonight, I do not know," said former Crystal Palace forward Clinton Morrison.

"He must be thinking, 'What do I have to do? We have injuries to two of the star players up front, and I'm still not getting on the pitch'."

Estevao will be hoping he can follow in the footsteps of Neto and revive his Stamford Bridge career.

Sports.title: Red Roses: Ellie Kildunne named on bench for second England match in a row
Sports.text:
Ellie Kildunne has been named on the England bench for their fixture against the USA, despite head coach John Mitchell making six changes to his side.

The 27-year-old full-back was dropped for the 31-22 defeat by Canada last Saturday, with Mitchell saying she needed to show "greater consistency".

Despite the loss in Ottawa, Bristol Bears star Kildunne will once again have to settle for a place on the bench for Friday's match against the USA in New Jersey, with Emma Sing retaining her spot.

With 67 England caps to her name, Kildunne was named World Rugby's player of the year in 2024, and starred in the Red Roses' 2025 World Cup victory.

Four of Mitchell's changes are to the backs, with Tatyana Heard, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Flo Robinson and Holly Aitchison handed their first starts of the tour, while forwards Mackenzie Carson and Maud Muir replace Hannah Botterman and Sarah Bern.

"Our intent is to start this next phase strongly against the USA, with six months until our next Test in the Women's Six Nations," said Mitchell.

"We're rotating some positions this week to refresh the group, create opportunities and continue building our depth.

"Selection is driven by what the team needs against the USA, the behaviours we value and the performance we're preparing to deliver.

"Everyone has a role, and everyone is accountable for our standards."

Sports.title: Sergio Perez signs multi-year extension with Cadillac
Sports.text:
Sergio Perez will remain with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a multi-year contract extension.

The 36-year-old, who is set to celebrate his 300th Grand Prix start in his home race in Mexico City this weekend, joined the American Formula One team last August before their debut season on the grid, racing alongside fellow veteran Valtteri Bottas.

Perez made his Formula One debut in 2011 and has won six grands prix – five for Red Bull between 2021-24 and one for Racing Point (now Aston Martin) in 2020.

He finished third in the 2022 drivers' championship and second behind team-mate Max Verstappen in 2023.

Despite having two years left on his contract, he was dropped by Red Bull at the end of the 2024 season after the team felt he had run out of time to prove he could support Verstappen.

Perez sits bottom of the 2026 standings, with three 14th-place finishes – in Barcelona, Silverstone, and Azerbaijan – his best performances. Neither he nor Bottas has earned a point for Cadillac.

"Joining Cadillac from day one was a project I truly believed in, and extending my commitment feels like a natural continuation of this chapter," said Perez.

"Building a Formula One team from the ground up takes time, relentless work and patience, but the progress we are making together is incredibly rewarding.

"There is still a lot of work ahead of us and I am fully committed to the next three years."

Sports.title: Chelsea Women: How unbeaten Blues are getting back to their best
Sports.text:
Chelsea's 2-0 victory over Roma in the Women's Champions League was yet another demonstration they can win in different ways.

Sonia Bompastor's side disappointed last season when they lost their Women's Super League and FA Cup crowns, while rivals Arsenal handed them an exit from Europe at the quarter-final stage.

That followed a dream unbeaten season in which the Blues wrapped up a domestic treble in Bompastor's first year in charge.

Having previously won six successive WSL titles, a blip was inevitable and their transition period highlighted flaws in the new era under their French boss.

There was still optimism in this campaign and, while Bompastor expected it would take more time, Chelsea have started impressively.

They are unbeaten in all competitions, top of the Women's Super League with Manchester City after seven games, and have won two and drawn one of their opening three Champions League phase matches.

"I'm really pleased with the results for sure, but not only the results, I think the different performances," said Bompastor earlier this week.

"Right now, the way we are performing gives us a really good advantage and a big chance to win games."

Their 2-0 victory over Roma on Wednesday was well deserved.

A flurry of chances were squandered in a dominant first half before substitute Ellie Carpenter broke the deadlock after 51 minutes.

Chelsea made sure of victory when defender Kadeisha Buchanan nodded in their second just before the end.

"I'm really pleased with the solid performances in terms of the defensive aspects. We have played three games and we haven't conceded," added Bompastor.

"When you want to go far in competitions, it's good to have this solid base. With the quality we have in the team, I'm confident we will always create opportunities."

She admitted the Champions League was "a different level" to what they had already overcome in the WSL and Bompastor has rotated her squad effectively to cope in both competitions.

They seem to have sorted out their defensive leaks that were so evident last season and look more clinical going forward.

Full-back Carpenter has four goals in all competitions, England forward Lauren James is in scintillating form and young midfielder Lexi Potter is developing a flourishing partnership with Lionesses star Keira Walsh.

They look unpredictable, being able to adapt shape in a back three or a back four, and can go direct with the aid of goalkeeper Hannah Hampton's distribution.

They had to grind out their win over Roma in a way that former boss Emma Hayes' sides used to do - proof in itself they have learned from the previous campaign.

"Even when we opened the competition against Austria Vienna, it was a tough game because they were brave and exposed us to some challenges," said Bompastor.

"We found a way to win, but obviously we want to control every game as much as we can, no matter what competition it is.

"Tonight and on Sunday we rotated the team a little bit. We find different ways to impose ourselves in the game and to score goals. That's good."

Manchester City won the WSL title impressively last season but externally, there was an expectation Chelsea would bounce back.

Bompastor was more cautious, insisting they were still transitioning after the departures of big-name players including Sam Kerr, Millie Bright and Guro Reiten.

She said: "You need to consider the fact that Chelsea had the same coach for 12 years. It takes a while for players to adjust to a new coach, a new way of playing and a philosophy.

"Even if you have really good players, it doesn't just go like this. There are a lot of things we are doing behind the scenes for us to stay successful.

"I was lucky enough to come in when [Hayes] left the team in a really good place. But last season we had a year where a lot of important players left."

But captain Erin Cuthbert said she was "not really" surprised at how good their level has been so far.

"We had a good time to build in pre-season and a good trip away. The quality was always there, we just weren't clicking," she added.

"Manchester City ran away with the league in the end, but we were there or thereabouts. I feel this time the team's just gone up another level."

As well as adapting more to Bompastor's ways, and adding defensive solidity to a creative frontline, work has gone into improving the club's culture.

Cuthbert said before Wednesday's win there was "really good momentum and a good feeling" in the squad - so can they kick on now?

"For me, the mental aspects and cultural aspects are just as important," admitted Bompastor.

"We probably needed to rebuild a little bit of that going into this new season. We reflected a lot on how we wanted to set up the process for that.

"Right now, we are in a good place. When you are able to get good results, it's not only about the tactical aspects. It also has to be about mentality, culture and values.

"I think we have clarity on where we want to go as a team and how we want to get there, and that's just as important."

Sports.title: Justin Tucker: Kansas City Chiefs defend decision to sign kicker to practice squad
Sports.text:
Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid has defended the decision to sign Justin Tucker to their practice squad, stating the kicker has "done his suspension".

Tucker, one of the most accurate kickers in NFL history, was last year accused of sexual misconduct, external by 16 massage therapists in the Baltimore area during the 2010s.

The 36-year-old - who won Super Bowl XLVII with the Baltimore Ravens - has consistently denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges.

Following an investigation, Tucker received a 10-game suspension, external from the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy.

He was released by Baltimore in May 2025 in what they described as a "football decision" following declining form.

Having served the ban last season, Tucker is immediately available for selection.

Reid said in a news conference on Wednesday: "He's done his suspension, taking care of that business there. I'll leave it at that.

"We try to do our homework the best way we possibly can and talk to a lot of people, make sure things are okay."

Pressed on what he meant by "homework", Reid added: "I'm not going to get into all that. To bring him here, I did some homework.

"He's here and he's on the practice squad, so we roll with it."

Tucker, a five-time All-Pro, is second in NFL history in field-goal percentage, making 89.1% of his attempts across 13 seasons, but endured the worst season of his career in 2024, kicking just 73.3% of his field-goal attempts.

The Chiefs made their move for him following a run of poor form by Harrison Butker, who has been the team's kicker since 2017 and has the fifth-best accuracy (87.3%) in NFL history.

However, the 31-year-old has missed five of his 16 field-goal attempts this season, including two from three in a 20-3 defeat by the Seattle Seahawks on Saturday.

Sports.title: Carabao Cup: 'Stutter' penalty back under debate after Barco miss costs Chelsea
Sports.text:
The pros and cons of a stuttering run-up are under debate after two crucial penalty misses in the Carabao Cup last 16.

Chelsea midfielder Valentin Barco missed the Blues' fourth penalty in their entertaining shootout defeat by Liverpool when he hit the post after a stuttered run-up.

Xabi Alonso's side would be in the EFL Cup quarter-finals had he scored, but they crashed out as defender Wesley Fofana sent one in sudden death high into the Kop at Anfield.

Barco's miss came after Arsenal midfielder Bruno Guimaraes had his spot-kick saved after a similar 'stutter' run-up as the Gunners crashed out against League Two Fleetwood Town on Tuesday night.

Both were shown how to do it by Liverpool defender Joe Gomez - a player who has never scored a senior goal in 319 professional appearances - who rifled the winning penalty into the top corner after a simple run-up.

Players opt for the stutter in a bid to trick the goalkeeper into giving them a clue as to which way they will dive.

The problem is it can backfire spectacularly if the goalkeeper holds their nerve or - in Barco's case - the taker fails to hit the target.

Former Chelsea defender Cesar Azpilicueta told ITV: "Every player picks his style where he feels confident, and for Valentin Barco, I believe that is his way of shooting it. I don't believe that was his first time, I hope not!"

The 'stutter' penalty became a theme of this year's World Cup. There were 26 at the summer's tournament but 11 were missed.

The stop-start run-up technique does not have a strict definition but a player is allowed, under Fifa rules, to stop or feint in the run-up as long as they don't do it directly before kicking the ball.

Even Harry Kane tried it in the summer and missed. His stuttering run-up led to Croatia goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic saving his penalty in England's 4-2 win.

But because Livakovic came off his line early, Kane got a retake and smashed it home with a straightforward approach.

Arsenal and Brazil midfielder Guimaraes was one of those 11 to miss at the World Cup but did not change his approach at Fleetwood.

Some players have used it to their advantage. Brazil icon Pele was famous for it while Cristiano Ronaldo has used it with both success and failure.

Manchester United's Bruno Fernandes, former Chelsea and Arsenal midfielder Jorginho and Wolves striker Raul Jimenez are others who often use the 'stutter' style.

"I wouldn't allow it if I was a manager," former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told TalkSport on Wednesday after Arsenal's defeat the night before.

"It is ridiculous, self-indulgence, a player trying to be the centre of attention.

"When they do the stutter they think the keeper might go, but they aren't going that early, they aren't being tricked any more. It is naive."

But former Liverpool and Chelsea full-back Glen Johnson had a different view and pointed to the fact that Barco missed by mere inches.

"I like the technique," he told ITV. "It gives the players a bit of time.

"W what confused me about that one [from Barco] is usually players are watching the keeper. He has moved, he has got it right and gone the right way but lifted it in the air for no reason.

"You have the whole goal to shoot at and that is the surprising part. He has already beaten the goalkeeper, he doesn't have to hit it into the top corner.

"If he puts that ball three inches to the right you would say it is the best penalty you have seen."

Sports.title: South Africa vs Australia: Marnus Labuschagne hits record low but new guard stand up for tourists
Sports.text:
Third Test, Cape Town (day two of five)

South Africa 329: Ackerman 95; Starc 6-72

Australia 330-4: Inglis 85*; Jansen 2-37

Australia lead by one run

Marnus Labuschagne has been front and centre for an era of Australian cricket.

Chirping, chewing and, with bat in hand, often appearing to idolise and mimic his team-mate Steve Smith.

Smith has been ruled out of the enthralling decisive Test against South Africa with a neck injury.

Without him, Australia wanted their number three to feast at last chance saloon, where he has been perched for an eternity, on day two in Cape Town.

The 32-year-old lasted five deliveries and did not score a run.

Labuschagne failed to scored a Test century for the 48th time in a row - a new record for the number of consecutive innings a batter in Australia’s top four has waited to raise his bat at three figures.

"That will never be broken," said former Australia quick Jason Gillespie on ABC.

"I say that because, respectfully, I don't think anyone will be given that length of time again."

There was a time when, from his insertion into the 2019 Ashes as a concussion substitute until the end of England's next quest to win back the urn, Labuschagne averaged 65 in Test cricket.

Repeat that over a Test career and only Sir Donald Bradman's mark of 99.94 would be ahead.

Instead, since his last Test century at Old Trafford in 2023, he averages 24.77.

Labuschagne may get one more chance in this Test, should Australia not progress from their position of 330-4, leading by one run, and dismiss South Africa before needing to pad up again.

Even that may not be enough.

"I just feel it is too far gone now," Gillespie added. "It is a very big sample size. Australia are at a point where they need to look elsewhere."

Labuschagne's technique has been pored over again and again as his slump progressed.

In August, the great Ricky Ponting, one of his predecessors as Australia's number three, called for the axe to fall.

"He can't score off the back foot," was Ponting's cutting remark.

Having batted nicely in three or four innings in this series only to give it away after reaching 30, here he was stuck on the crease, playing back to a full ball and nicking spinner Simon Harmer to slip.

"That's nerves and the pressure the selectors have put him under for an extended period of time," said former Australia batter Simon Katich on SEN Radio.

"They put him in this position by not making the decision to give him a breather."

It felt like all of Labuschagne's issues collapsing into one.

But if his pained stare down the pitch signalled the end of something, what followed hinted at their future.

With Travis Head already out and Labuschagne following, the score 58-2 in reply to the Proteas' 329, there was no Smith to steer Australia out of this tricky spot.

Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, three of the junior members of this side, instead made fifties and put their side in the ascendancy.

Renshaw is one of those who has been kept out by the selectors in the hope Labuschagne could rediscover his best form.

Had he been picked to open in the World Test Championship final against South Africa in 2025, rather than Australia's decision to try Labuschagne as opener, he may have spent the following 17 months ending the debate over who should replace David Warner.

Having got his chance in this series, initially as number five before the Nic Maddinson experiment was cut short after two Tests, the Middlesbrough-born Renshaw looks like being a fixture for this winter and beyond.

His 74 here, which followed a career-best 190 in Durban, suggests a return to England next summer awaits.

Green is one who has not lacked opportunity. Long viewed as Australia's golden boy, the 27-year-old has flicked across 39 previous Test without ever truly appearing comfortable.

In making 65 below Table Mountain, the towering all-rounder played with the composure and authority he has often lacked.

Most impressive, though, was Inglis - another Aussie who spent his early years in Yorkshire.

He had not faced the red ball since March, has had his preparations limited by a broken finger, and came in with South Africa buoyed by Marco Jansen dismissing Renshaw and Green in successive overs before tea.

The 31-year-old finished 85 not out in an unbroken partnership of 145 with Alex Carey. There would be no late-evening South Africa fightback, like the one Mitchell Starc inspired on day one to bowl South Africa out.

This is not to say everything has fallen into place for Australia. Smith will return, meaning Green and Inglis would likely move from their current batting positions of four and five for their next Test against New Zealand in December.

Smith has avoided batting in Labuschagne's position before, and a four-Test trial of Green in that spot in 2024 and 2025 was aborted after he returned 188 across eight innings.

Leeds-born Inglis, meanwhile, has three first-class matches worth experience at number three, in which he averaged 12.66 and has a best score of 29.

But if ever a day showed Australia there is merit in moving from one generation to another it was this.

Three of their less experienced players, albeit two of them have celebrated their 30th birthdays, stood up to take Australia to a position from which they can control this Test.

Labuschagne did not. His days look numbered.

Sports.title: Novak Djokovic battles to 'big' comeback win over Ugo Humbert in Basel
Sports.text:
Novak Djokovic pulled off a hard-fought comeback victory over Ugo Humbert on his first appearance in Basel for 15 years.

Battling in the final months of the year to keep alive his chances of qualifying for the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin, Djokovic celebrated what he viewed as a "big win" by overcoming Frenchman Ugo Humbert 4-6 6-3 6-4.

The men's record 24-time major winner blasted a forehand winner down the line to end the contest after two and a half hours.

It ensured Djokovic, 11th in the race to Turin, remains in the hunt for a record 19th appearance at the ATP Finals, for which only the year's top eight performers qualify.

The 39-year-old beat great rival Roger Federer to win the Basel title in 2009, and had not played at the event since 2011.

"I was under attack from the very first point and had to weather the storm," Djokovic said.

"It's my first indoor match, so I expected to be a little bit rusty in a tough draw. It is a big win for me, I know there are quite a few things I can do better but a win is a win, and I will take that today."

Gaming_Tech.title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
Gaming_Tech.text:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.

On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).

Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.

Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.

The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.

Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres.

Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.

Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.

The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.

The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."

Gaming_Tech.title: Elon Musk a 'real genius', Putin says after talks with SpaceX boss
Gaming_Tech.text:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.

The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.

"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."

Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.

Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.

The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".

"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.

Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.

US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.

Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.

Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".

Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.

Gaming_Tech.title: Drone technology: Start-ups look for ways to make quieter drones
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland.

She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads.

It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders.

"They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant.

"You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says.

Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.

Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.

Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.

Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.

While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.

Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.

"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.

Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?

One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.

The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.

Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.

Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.

Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.

For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.

He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – except that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.

"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"

The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.

"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

Gaming_Tech.title: iPhone Duo: Apple to replace handsets affected by screen issues
Gaming_Tech.text:
Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.

Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.

Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.

The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.

Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.

The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using AI.

Francisco Jeronimo, technology analyst at market research firm IDC, said that meant some caution was needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run.

But he added the early reports of issues also showed "that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables".

Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO
Gaming_Tech.text:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.

Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.

Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.

The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

Gaming_Tech.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
Gaming_Tech.text:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

Gaming_Tech.title: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?
Gaming_Tech.text:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side programming language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.

Governments and cyber-security agencies rushed to contain the fallout, urging website owners to check if their sites were affected and, if so, install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.

But in the days since the issues came to light, disruption to sites and services has continued to ripple around the world.

Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.

It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server.

Developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, PHP still powers lots of platforms today, including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites.

When you visit a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.

It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.

According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.

It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation, external, composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity".

A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet.

Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws were inherent in the language itself, affecting versions of PHP released over the last decade.

The technical bugs, given the technical IDs CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were ranked a 9.2 out of 10 in severity by researchers.

Calif researcher Ryan Austin, who helped uncover it, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found".

Wiz wrote in a blog post, external about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the bugs to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed.

AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.

He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.

Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites.

The alert on 21 October disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.

It included Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.

Sites and pages were also taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and some BBC pages, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website on Wednesday.

But while many sites were back up by Thursday, others were still being taken down temporarily elsewhere as people and businesses check for potential exposure.

The UK Government revealed on Thursday some "limited" services may be offline temporarily.

It said 32 sites had been taken down as a precaution, none of them large public-facing services.

In France, telecommunications company Orange also said it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

On Friday, local media in Japan reported telecom operator SoftBank Corp had temporarily suspended emergency alerts for earthquakes, tsunamis and other disasters.

According to the Mainichi newspaper, external, SoftBank customers have been urged to make sure they have other ways to get alerts about natural disasters - with its mobile phone alerts not set to sound even in the event of a strong earthquake.

The service is reportedly set to resume on Monday.

Some experts warn the issue could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.

More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, said cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere of UNSW Sydney.

The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.

Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations, external that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.

"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.

Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP in posts on X.

Tech companies also sought to quickly secure their systems.

E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue, but its websites were operating as normal.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, also said it had seen "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, external.

As of Friday morning, no successful attacks had been reported.

But experts have warned any impact may take time to become fully apparent.

And operators of a number of services where PHP may have been used - not just in web development - are still being urged to check their systems and implement updates, where necessary.

"It is important to remember that PHP is not limited to web applications," said Daniel Stewart, head of threat intelligence at global risk manager LRQA.

"It is commonly found in the management interfaces of network appliances, load balancers, and embedded devices, which are often overlooked during these incidents."

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches has climbed - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.

The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users - meaning most people won't need to take any action.

But small businesses with sites, including those built using WordPress, may be wondering how to protect themselves.

Those who own websites or manage infrastructure running PHP have been urged to secure their websites by updating to the latest version.

Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes - known as patching - is "a bit like running a Windows update".

If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied - something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins.

If you look after your website yourself, Munro says "it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied".

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends, external considering temporarily taking sites offline if updates or temporary protections cannot be applied quickly enough.

The US National Security Agency has also urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks, telling people to closely monitor updates from software vendors.

"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.

And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.
